faqs.answer: Yellow leaves often point to excess moisture around the roots, poor drainage, or sudden stress from relocation. Check for soggy soil, leaf drop, and soft stems. Consistent routines are important when caring for fiddleleaf fig.
faqs.question: Why are my fiddleleaf fig leaves turning yellow?

faqs.answer: This species naturally grows as a tree, not a compact plant. Indoors it can reach 1.8–3 m (6–10 ft) over time, while outdoor specimens in warm climates become much larger with age.
faqs.question: Does fiddleleaf fig grow tall or stay compact?

cutting.intro: Trim lightly to keep Ficus lyrata tidy and healthy.
bullets: Remove yellowing, torn, or spent leaves and any damaged growth to reduce stress.
Shorten leggy stems as needed for shape, using clean, disinfected pruners.
Check every 2–4 weeks and trim only small amounts between larger pruning sessions.

support.intro: Ficus lyrata may need light support checks as it grows taller indoors.
bullets: Check ties and loosen any that press into stems every 4–6 weeks.
Make sure stakes stay firm in the pot and guide leaning new growth gently.

aeration.intro: Light aeration helps if the potting mix surface starts to crust or compact.
bullets: Every 1–2 months, gently loosen the top 2–3 cm (0.8–1.2 in) with a stick or small fork.
Aerate when water pools on top briefly or the surface feels hard between waterings.

cleaning.intro: Clean the plant every 2–4 weeks to keep foliage working well.
bullets: Wipe leaves gently with a soft damp cloth, supporting each leaf by hand to avoid tearing.
Remove fallen debris and rinse the saucer and pot rim so dust, residue, and hiding spots do not build up.
This improves light absorption, reduces pest pressure, and keeps the plant looking tidy.

humidity.intro: Humidity support is only sometimes needed for Ficus lyrata indoors.
bullets: Check weekly; if air is dry, refill a pebble tray or run a humidifier to maintain 40–60% humidity.
Watch for crispy brown leaf edges or margins, which can suggest air that is too dry.

mulching.intro: Top-dressing is optional but useful for indoor Ficus lyrata in dry rooms.
bullets: Refresh a thin 1–2 cm (0.4–0.8 in) layer of fine bark or coco chips every 3–6 months.
It helps slow surface drying and buffers root-zone temperature slightly.

watering.intro: Water the fiddleleaf fig on a simple repeat schedule.
bullets: About every 6 days, water when the top 2–3 cm (1 in) feels dry or leaves start to droop slightly.
Soak the soil fully until excess drains out, then empty the saucer so roots do not sit in water.
Avoid the common mistake of adding small splashes too often, which keeps soil unevenly wet.

fertilize.intro: Feed fiddleleaf fig regularly during active growth.
bullets: Apply a balanced houseplant fertilizer at 1/2 strength every 4–6 weeks in spring and summer.
Add fertilizer to water and apply to already moist soil, not dry roots.
Pause or reduce feeding in autumn and winter if growth slows.
Avoid overfeeding, which can cause salt buildup and brown leaf edges.

repotting.intro: Check repotting needs regularly to avoid root stress.
bullets: Inspect every 6–12 months for roots at drainage holes, slowed growth, or water running straight through.
If needed, move up 1 pot size, about 5–8 cm (2–3 in) wider than the current pot.
Use a well-draining chunky mix and a pot with drainage holes.

inspection.intro: Set a closer hands-on inspection every 2–4 weeks.
bullets: Lift and turn leaves to inspect undersides, check the stem base, and look at drainage holes for roots or trapped moisture.
If roots crowd the pot, stems soften, or pests appear, isolate the plant and plan follow-up care or repotting.

monitoring.intro: Do a quick visual check each week between care tasks.
bullets: Look at leaf color and texture, new growth, soil moisture, and the overall surface for early pest signs.
If leaves dull, spot, droop, or growth stalls, adjust light or watering and inspect more closely.

careDetails.aboutPlant:
Ficus lyrata is a tropical ornamental tree grown indoors for its large, leathery leaves with a distinctive fiddle shape. It has an upright, tree-like habit and can become tall and architectural with age.

This species is native to western Africa, where it grows in warm, bright conditions. Indoors, its appeal comes with some challenge, as it reacts clearly to poor light, sudden changes, and inconsistent moisture.

For easier care for fiddleleaf fig, place it in bright, indirect light and use a well-draining mix that stays slightly moist but not soggy.

careAdvice.title: Rotate Gradually
careAdvice.description: Turn the pot 45° every 1–2 weeks during active growth so the canopy develops evenly, but avoid sudden moves to a much brighter or darker spot because this species often drops leaves after abrupt changes.

careAdvice.title: Clean Large Leaves
careAdvice.description: Wipe the leaves with a soft damp cloth every 2–4 weeks to remove dust so light reaches the leaf surface and early pest issues are easier to spot when caring for fiddleleaf fig.

careAdvice.title: Inspect For Pests
careAdvice.description: Check the undersides of leaves and the stem joints weekly for spider mites, scale, and mealybugs, since infestations often start in sheltered areas and spread quickly on broad foliage.

careAdvice.title: Stake Young Stems
careAdvice.description: Use a soft tie and a slim stake if a young plant leans, because upright support helps the trunk strengthen while growing fiddleleaf fig in containers with one-sided indoor light.

careAdvice.title: Flush Salt Buildup
careAdvice.description: Every 2–3 months, run room-temperature water through the pot for 30–60 seconds and let it drain fully to wash out accumulated fertilizer salts that can cause brown leaf edges.

soil.intro: Ficus lyrata needs an airy, moisture-retentive but fast-draining mix.
bullets: Use a chunky loam-based houseplant mix with organic matter such as peat or coco coir.
Add pine bark and perlite, or a little coarse sand, to improve airflow and drainage.
Keep pH at 6.0–7.0 and avoid dense, clay-heavy mixes that stay soggy.
Choose a structure that stays lightly moist without compacting around the roots.

water.intro: Steady moisture suits Ficus lyrata best.
bullets: Water when the top 2–3 cm (1 in) of soil feels dry, often about every 6 days in active growth.
Reduce frequency in winter, and always use fast-draining soil and drainage holes to avoid standing water around roots.
Overwatering causes yellowing leaves and soft stems; underwatering causes drooping, dry edges, and early leaf drop.

soilPH.intro: Slightly acidic to neutral soil helps Ficus lyrata absorb nutrients reliably.
bullets: Aim for pH 6.0–7.0; it prefers slightly acidic to neutral conditions, not alkaline soil.
Test with a soil pH meter or kit; adjust low pH with garden lime and high pH with sulfur-based amendments.
Wrong pH can cause nutrient lock-out, pale new leaves, chlorosis, and slower growth even with regular feeding.

pruning.intro: Pruning helps Ficus lyrata stay balanced and manageable indoors.
bullets: Trim in spring or early summer when recovery and branching are strongest.
Remove dead, damaged, or crowded leaves and weak stems first.
Cut above a node with clean pruners to shape height and encourage fuller growth.

humidity.intro: Humidity matters for fiddleleaf fig, with best growth at 40–60%.
bullets: It tolerates somewhat dry indoor air but may show slower growth.
Low humidity can cause brown leaf edges, crisp patches, or leaf drop.
Raise humidity with a humidifier, pebble tray, or grouped plants.

sunlight.intro: Bright, indirect light keeps the fiddleleaf fig compact and healthy.
bullets: Aim for 6–8 hours daily, ideally near filtered east- or south-facing light with gentle morning sun.
It tolerates partial shade for short periods, but low light slows growth, stretches stems, and may cause leaf drop.
Protect from harsh afternoon sun, especially in summer; in winter, move closer to the window as daylight weakens.

container.intro: This species is well suited to container growing when the pot is stable and free-draining.
bullets: Use a pot with drainage holes and empty any saucer promptly so excess water leaves the root zone fast.
Give roots enough depth and width with a 30–40 cm (12–16 in) pot rather than a shallow planter.
Choose a heavier container material if needed, because Ficus lyrata can become top-heavy as foliage expands.

placement.intro: Place it indoors in strong filtered light or outdoors only in warm, bright shelter.
bullets: A fiddleleaf fig does best near an east- or south-facing window, set 30–60 cm (12–24 in) back if midday sun is intense.
Give a little space from walls and nearby plants so air moves freely around the leaves.
Avoid cold drafts, air conditioners, heating vents, and harsh direct midday sun that can scorch foliage.

fertilizer.intro: Fertilizer supports steady leaf growth in fiddleleaf fig during active growth.
bullets: Use a balanced houseplant fertilizer, compost-based feed, or slow-release formula.
Feed every 2–4 weeks in spring and summer at 1/2 strength dilution.
Reduce to every 6–8 weeks or stop in winter when growth slows.

winterCare.intro: Winter care matters because this tropical plant is not frost tolerant.
bullets: Keep it indoors at 18–27°C (64–81°F) near bright, indirect light.
Water less often but keep soil slightly moist, never soggy.
Move pots away from drafts, heaters, and cold glass to limit leaf drop.

propagation.intro: Propagation is usually done from seed, though indoor success is limited.
bullets: Sow seeds in spring in a warm, bright setup with indirect light.
Use a moist, well-draining medium and keep it evenly moist, not wet.
Maintain 21–27°C (70–81°F) and moderate humidity until seedlings establish.

temperature.intro: Warm, stable conditions support steady growth.
bullets: Best growth occurs at 65–81°F (18–27°C), with little day-to-night fluctuation.
Avoid prolonged exposure below 55°F (13°C); cold drafts can trigger leaf drop, and frost can severely damage foliage.
It handles brief heat above 86°F (30°C) if light and moisture are balanced, but extreme heat dries leaves faster.

repottingAndTransplanting.intro: Repotting helps maintain root health and steady growth indoors.
bullets: Move up when roots circle the pot, drainage slows, or growth becomes weak.
Repot in spring every 2–3 years into a pot 2–5 cm (1–2 in) wider.
Keep the root ball intact, use fresh chunky mix, and water lightly after repotting.

facts.text: In its native west African range, this species often begins life high in the canopy as a hemiepiphyte and later sends roots down toward the ground. This growth habit helps explain its strong need for bright light indoors.
facts.title: Rainforest hemiepiphyte

facts.text: Its large leaves are shaped like a lyre or violin, which is the source of the species name lyrata and the common name fiddle-leaf fig. The leaf shape makes this fig easy to recognize among cultivated houseplants.
facts.title: Violin-shaped leaves

facts.text: This species belongs to the fig and mulberry family, Moraceae. Like other figs, it produces a specialized enclosed inflorescence called a syconium rather than a typical open flower.
facts.title: Moraceae relative

interestingFacts.didYouKnow: Ficus lyrata has received the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit, a recognition given to plants considered especially reliable and valuable in cultivation.

pestsAndDiseases.name: Spider mites
pestsAndDiseases.solution: Wipe both sides of the leaves, rinse the plant thoroughly, and repeat with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil every 7–10 days until activity stops. Raise humidity to 40–60% and keep the plant away from heating vents to reduce repeat outbreaks.
pestsAndDiseases.description: These tiny pests are common on indoor plants kept in dry air and often feed on the undersides of leaves. Symptoms include fine webbing, pale speckling, and gradual leaf yellowing or drop.

pestsAndDiseases.name: Scale insects
pestsAndDiseases.solution: Remove visible insects by hand or with a cotton swab dipped in alcohol, then wash the foliage and stems carefully. Follow with horticultural oil, making sure to cover hidden areas along stems and leaf joints, and repeat as needed.
pestsAndDiseases.description: These insects attach to stems and leaves and feed on sap, which can weaken growth over time. Symptoms include sticky residue, brown or tan bumps, yellowing leaves, and reduced vigor.

pestsAndDiseases.name: Mealybugs
pestsAndDiseases.solution: Isolate the plant, remove visible insects with alcohol on a swab, and clean the plant thoroughly, especially where leaves join the stem. Repeat treatment with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil at 7–10 day intervals until no new insects appear.
pestsAndDiseases.description: These insects gather in leaf axils and along stems, where they appear as white, cottony clusters. They weaken the plant by feeding on sap and may also leave sticky honeydew.

pestsAndDiseases.name: Bacterial leaf spot
pestsAndDiseases.solution: Remove affected leaves with clean tools and avoid wetting the foliage during watering. Improve airflow, keep the plant in bright indirect light, and water the soil only when the top 2–3 cm (1 in) feels dry.
pestsAndDiseases.description: This disease causes dark, water-soaked or irregular spots on leaves, sometimes with yellow halos. It is more likely when foliage stays wet and air movement is poor.

pestsAndDiseases.name: Anthracnose
pestsAndDiseases.solution: Trim off badly affected leaves, discard fallen debris, and keep water off the foliage. Improve spacing and airflow, maintain steady watering without waterlogging, and refresh the potting mix if the plant has been kept too damp for long periods.
pestsAndDiseases.description: This fungal disease can cause brown to black leaf lesions, especially along edges or tips, and damaged areas may expand in warm, humid conditions. Stressed plants are more likely to show repeated spotting.

faqs.question: Warum werden die Blätter meiner Geigenfeige gelb?

faqs.answer: Diese Art wächst natürlich als Baum, nicht als kompakte Pflanze. Drinnen kann sie im Laufe der Zeit 1,8–3 m (6–10 ft) erreichen, während Außenexemplare in warmen Klimazonen mit dem Alter viel größer werden.
